title: Regression and the Normal Distribution — Quiz
description: 10 multiple-choice questions spanning recall, understanding, analysis, and expert difficulty, covering Sections 1.1-1.6 of the chapter excerpt.

questions.question: According to Section 1.1, what is the distinguishing feature of regression analysis?
options: Its ability to randomly assign treatments to subjects
Its ability to make statements about a variable of interest after controlling for known explanatory variables
Its requirement that all data be collected experimentally
Its reliance exclusively on graphical rather than numerical summaries
questions.explanation: The text states regression's distinguishing feature is making statements about variables after controlling for known explanatory variables. Option A describes experimental design, a different (though related) statistical activity mentioned earlier in 1.1, not regression's defining feature.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: How many adult children's heights appear in Galton's 1885 dataset referenced in Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: Table 1.1 totals 928 adult children. 272 is the bodily injury claims sample size (Section 1.2), and 1,340 is the AutoBI exercise sample size (Section 1.8) — both from elsewhere in the chapter.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: In the normal curve density f(y), what role do mu and sigma^2 play?
options: mu is the scale parameter and sigma^2 is the location parameter
mu is the location parameter and sigma^2 is the scale parameter
Both are location parameters
Both are scale parameters
questions.explanation: The text explicitly says mu and sigma^2 (mean and median) are known as the location and scale parameters, respectively — mu controls location (center), sigma^2 controls the degree of peakedness/spread.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: For the Massachusetts bodily injury claims example, the average logarithmic claim was 0.481. What dollar amount does this correspond to?
questions.explanation: The text computes 1000*exp(0.481) = $1,617.77 as the dollar equivalent of the mean log-claim. $50,000 is instead cited as the largest raw claim, and $3,912 confuses the log-scale maximum (3.912) with a dollar figure.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: In the Box-Cox family of power transforms, what does y^(lambda) reduce to when lambda = 0?
options: y itself
ln(y)
sqrt(y)
questions.explanation: The text defines y^(lambda) = (y^lambda - 1)/lambda for lambda != 0, and ln(y) specifically when lambda = 0. sqrt(y) corresponds to lambda = 1/2, a different named case in the same family, not the lambda=0 case.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: Which best describes a right-skewed (positively skewed) distribution as defined in Section 1.3?
options: A longer tail on the left with mass concentrated on the right
A longer tail on the right with mass concentrated on the left
A perfectly symmetric bell shape
A distribution with no tails at all
questions.explanation: The text defines right/positively skewed as having a longer tail on the right and greater concentration of mass to the left — the opposite pattern (long left tail, mass on the right) is what the text calls left-skewed/negatively skewed.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four Basic Sampling Assumptions listed in Section 1.4?
options: E(y_i) = mu
Var(y_i) = sigma^2
{y_i} are independent
{y_i} were collected via a designed experiment
questions.explanation: The four listed assumptions are E(y_i)=mu, Var(y_i)=sigma^2, independence, and normality. Whether data come from a designed experiment or observational study is a separate topic (Section 1.5), not one of the four Basic Sampling Assumptions.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: Why is normality (Assumption 4) described as 'not required for many statistical inference procedures'?
options: Because normality is always true in practice
Because central limit theorems provide approximate normality for many statistics of interest
Because sample sizes are always too small for normality to matter
Because actuarial data is never continuous
questions.explanation: The text explicitly attributes this to central limit theorems, which yield approximate normality of many statistics even without the raw-data normality assumption. The other options are not claims made in the source.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: In the RAND Health Insurance Experiment described in Section 1.5, what made it a 'designed study' rather than observational?
options: Households volunteered for whichever plan they preferred
Households were randomly assigned to one of 14 insurance plans
Only healthy households were included
Data were collected from insurance company records after the fact
questions.explanation: The text states enrolled households were randomly assigned to one of 14 different insurance plans, which is the hallmark of a designed/experimental study with control over the treatment assignment, unlike observational data such as Galton's.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

questions.question: What actuarial problem does regression-based risk classification pricing primarily address, per Section 1.6?
options: Solvency testing
Adverse selection
The Central Limit Theorem's assumptions
Box-Cox transformation selection
questions.explanation: Section 1.6 explains that flat-rate pricing invites adverse selection (good risks leave, bad risks stay), and that regression-based classification lets each insured pay a fair, risk-based share, addressing this specific problem — distinct from reserving/solvency testing, the other two traditional actuarial areas mentioned.
sources: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex
